cards.text: Isaiah 60 just promised Zion a sunrise, with the LORD as her everlasting light (Isaiah 60:19). Now, in the book of Isaiah the prophet, someone new speaks: "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me". Anointed, friend, and that means there's a job to do.

cards.question: First job: the anointed speaker is sent to preach good news. Who is it for?

cards.text: And He's got a whole list, and it is NOT "call the bank back, renew the car registration." Every line on this list is for somebody who's hurting.

cards.question: Next on the list are the brokenhearted. What is the speaker sent to do for them?
True or false: the speaker is also sent to proclaim freedom to the prisoners.

cards.text: Then two things get proclaimed side by side: the LORD's favor, and our God's vengeance. And each one comes with a length of time.

cards.question: The speaker proclaims the LORD's favor and our God's vengeance. How long does each one get?

answers.text: A year of favor and a day of vengeance
A day of favor and a year of vengeance
A week of favor and a week of vengeance

cards.text: Hundreds of years later, Jesus stands up in the synagogue in Nazareth, reads these lines, and stops right after the year of the Lord's favor. Then He says, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing." (Luke 4:16-21)

cards.question: Back in Isaiah, the list keeps going. For all who mourn, what is the speaker sent to do?

cards.text: Then come three swaps for the mourners in Zion: ashes, mourning and a spirit of despair are all on the way out. I know swaps, friend. Mother Miller once swapped a worn-out stamper for a shiny new one, and I was NOT the shiny one.

cards.question: Instead of ashes, what does the speaker give the mourners in Zion?
True or false: in place of a spirit of despair, the mourners get a garment of praise.

cards.text: And these mourners won't stay bent over. They get a new title, something tall and strong, planted by the LORD Himself.

cards.question: What will the comforted mourners in Zion be called?
The LORD plants these oaks of righteousness. Why?

answers.text: So they may rule the nations

cards.text: OAKS, friend. Not a little houseplant on a windowsill, OAKS. And look at what these oaks of righteousness face: ancient ruins, places long devastated.

cards.question: What will the oaks of righteousness do with those ancient ruins?
True or false: the ruined cities they renew have only been in ruins for a few years.

cards.text: Ruins from many generations, rebuilt. And the farm work gets covered too: strangers feed the flocks, and foreigners plow the fields and tend the vines.

cards.question: With others tending the flocks and fields, what will God's people be called?
True or false: God's people will have to hand their riches over to the nations.

cards.text: Now shame and humiliation are on the way out. And something better is coming in their place.

cards.question: Instead of shame, what will God's people have?

cards.text: A DOUBLE portion in their land, and everlasting joy on top of it. Friend, I used to lose my mind when a cookie came out with TWO extra chocolate chips.
Then the LORD says why: "I, the LORD, love justice", and He hates robbery and iniquity.

cards.question: In His faithfulness, what will the LORD make with His people?

cards.text: And it doesn't stop with them: their descendants will be known among the nations. Me? I was known by one kitchen and the dead batteries I shared a drawer with.

cards.question: When people from the nations see these descendants, what will they acknowledge?

cards.text: Then the speaker cannot hold it in: "I will rejoice greatly in the LORD, my soul will exult in my God". That's not a polite golf clap, friend, that's hop-around-the-bakery joy.

cards.question: Why is the speaker rejoicing so greatly in God?

answers.text: God gave me a long life
God made me a great king

cards.text: The speaker is also wrapped in a robe of righteousness. Then comes a picture of what that outfit is like: people dressing up for one of the biggest days of their lives.

cards.question: Being wrapped in a robe of righteousness is like what?

answers.text: A bridegroom and a bride dressed up
A king dressed for his crowning

cards.text: A bride getting ready hits home in my bakery, since Revelation 19:7 says the Lamb's bride "has made herself ready." Now the last picture in Isaiah 61: a garden, where the earth brings forth its growth and seed springs up.

cards.question: As a garden makes seed spring up, what will the Lord GOD cause to spring up before all the nations?

findings.problem: The passage never says who the 'Me' of Isaiah 61:1 is, or whether the 'I' who rejoices in 61:10 is the same person. The cards call him 'someone new' and later 'the speaker,' which treats the 61:10 voice as the same person as in 61:1. One rule says to name a first-person speaker before quoting him. Another says to leave open what the text leaves open. The two rules pull in opposite directions here.
findings.question: When a passage's first-person speaker is unidentified, like Isaiah 61:1 and 61:10, should Papa Dorin name him? Or should he keep a neutral label like 'the speaker'? And may he treat the speakers in 61:1 and 61:10 as the same person?

findings.problem: This story card tells no part of Isaiah 61:1 beyond the fact that there is a list. It also says every line on the list is for somebody who's hurting. The list includes 'the day of our God's vengeance' (61:2), so that claim stretches the text.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: 'Every line on this list is for somebody who's hurting' overstates the text. The list also proclaims the day of our God's vengeance (Isaiah 61:2).

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Choosing between 'a year of favor and a day of vengeance' and its reverse means guessing the passage's wording. Nothing in card 6 lets the baker reason it out. Card 6 also calls 'year' and 'day' a 'length of time,' which is an interpretation the text doesn't state.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Hurry them along' sounds casual and modern next to 'Comfort them' and 'Correct them,' so it doesn't match the tone of the other answers.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Card 13 sets up the new title as 'something tall and strong, planted by the LORD Himself.' The wrong answer 'Cedars of Lebanon' fits that setup just as well. Psalm 104:16 even calls them 'the cedars of Lebanon that He planted.' A baker could argue it's right, and picking between oaks and cedars comes down to luck.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: Stop 1 has 7 multiple choice cards, 2 true or false cards and no fill in the blank cards. Multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin, and Stop 2 repeats the same pattern.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Story card 1 already says the ruins are 'ancient ruins, places long devastated.' That gives away the answer to card 3's true or false question about whether the ruins are only a few years old.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The question says 'people from the nations' see the descendants. Isaiah 61:9 says 'All who see them,' which is wider than the nations.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: Stop 2 has 8 multiple choice cards, 2 true or false cards and no fill in the blank cards. Multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin, and the stop repeats Stop 1's pattern.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Many story cards read like plain narration with no punch: Stop 1 cards 6 and 13, and Stop 2 cards 4, 7, 10 and 16. The few jokes are mild. The double portion line in Stop 2 card 9 lands softly. The walkthrough rarely reaches laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
